definition: The repeating building block of an NVIDIA GPU: a cluster of CUDA cores, four tensor cores, a register file and its own L1/shared memory. An H100 has 132 SMs and a Rubin GPU 224.

NVIDIA's name for a simple arithmetic lane in an SM that does one scalar operation (such as a 32-bit multiply-add) per clock. Thousands of them handle general parallel code; matrix math goes to the tensor cores instead.
A group of 32 GPU threads that execute the same instruction in lockstep on an SM. It is the unit the hardware schedules, so code that keeps all 32 threads busy runs fastest.
A group of SMs that share some scheduling and routing hardware. Rubin has eight GPCs holding 224 SMs; Hopper's H100 enables 132 SMs across its GPCs.

NVIDIA's combination of tensor-core hardware and software libraries that picks number formats (FP8 from Hopper, FP4/NVFP4 from Blackwell) and per-tensor or per-block scale factors automatically so models can run in lower precision without losing accuracy.
The fastest storage on a GPU: 256 KB of registers per SM holding the values threads are working on right now. It sits next to the arithmetic units and feeds them every clock.

Fast on-chip SRAM inside each SM (256 KB on H100 and B200, split between L1 cache and programmer-managed shared memory) where a kernel stages tiles of a matrix so the tensor cores can reuse them many times.
The last on-chip memory level, shared by all SMs: 50 MB on H100 and ~126 MB on B200. It catches data on its way from HBM so repeated reads do not use scarce HBM bandwidth.
A 256 KB per-SM scratchpad introduced with Blackwell that holds tensor-core accumulators and operands, freeing registers and keeping the larger tensor cores fed.
A Hopper-era hardware unit that copies whole tiles of a tensor between HBM/L2 and shared memory in the background, so threads can keep computing instead of issuing individual loads.
One operation that computes a × b + c in a single step; it counts as two floating-point operations. Matrix multiplication is almost entirely FMAs.

A grid of multiply-accumulate cells through which data flows in a fixed rhythm, each cell passing results to its neighbour. Google's TPU matrix units are 128×128 or 256×256 systolic arrays: very efficient for large matrices, less flexible for odd shapes.

Groq's inference chip design, licensed by NVIDIA in December 2025, that keeps model weights in on-chip SRAM (about 500 MB per chip) instead of HBM, trading capacity for very high bandwidth and low latency during decode.
Matrix-multiply units added to Intel Xeon CPU cores from Sapphire Rapids (2023) onward; each core can do up to 1,024 BF16 operations per clock, 16 times its vector units.
NVIDIA's die-to-die link that joins the two reticle-sized compute dies of a Blackwell or Rubin GPU at 10 TB/s, fast enough that software sees one GPU.

TSMC's CoWoS variant that replaces one large silicon interposer with a redistribution-layer interposer containing small embedded silicon bridges, allowing packages several reticles in size (used from Blackwell on).
A 19-bit tensor-core format introduced with Ampere that keeps FP32's range but only 10 mantissa bits, so FP32 code can use tensor cores without changes; values are still stored as 32 bits.
A 4-bit floating-point format (1 sign, 2 exponent and 1 mantissa bit) that can represent only eight magnitudes from 0 to 6; usable only with block scale factors such as MXFP4 or NVFP4.

An industry standard (Open Compute Project, 2023) in which each block of 32 low-precision values shares one 8-bit power-of-two scale factor. MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4 are the main members; NVIDIA's NVFP4 is a variant with 16-value blocks.

Vendors often quote 'sparse' peak throughput, which assumes 2:4 structured sparsity (half the weights zero) and is exactly twice the dense figure. Real models rarely run sparse, so this repo uses dense numbers.
